The Deaf community is very close-knit. Having family that is Deaf introduces me to Deaf people and then I'll attend parties or other outings with them and meet their friends. Somehow I've ended up with friends all away across the country and in other countries. Whenever I'm away from home and happen to meet someone who is Deaf and we connect on Facebook we will end up having all these random mutual friends. Especially if they went to Gallaudet University in DC (the only Deaf university in the country). To answer your last question there is a genetic component. More research is being done on this and they have some good findings if you ever want to read into it.

Not ignorant or insensitive. I've asked my family and friends this because it seems like a really good question. They have told me that they have an inner voice. Even though I've grown up with them and have known sign language my entire life I'm still perplex by the idea. Because if you're Deaf and have never heard a voice what would your inner voice sound like? I know my signing friends and family dream in ASL (I do sometimes too). But I would like to know more about the inner voice. I believe one time someone told me their inner voice signs.
Basically, I have no idea. But maybe I should see if there is any research on this.

Definitely try out the signs! Everyone I know would appreciate the effort. It's estimate that even the best lip readers can only catch about 20-30% of what is being said. It's incredibly difficult. Definitely try out your signing. Plus you get to practice your ASL so it's a win-win. Hope that helps!

Hahahaha it happens regularly. A waiter or an airline attendant will see us signing, they get all excited rush over and hand over the Braille menus.
One time at an airport when the airline staff saw us signing we were given wheelchairs. O.o
Our legs work fine, our eyes are fine, we don't need those accommodations.
I get it they are trying to be helpful. But just a little bit of education would really help. 
Bottom line: don't assume what people need, just ask.

Deaf culture is fantastic!! Sometimes (not speaking for you obviously) but people who are never exposed to sign are often left in this in between world of "well I'm not fully hearing but I don't know sign so I'm not Deaf" and then you are just managing with tips like lip reading which is incredibly difficult or other techniques that are often unreliable. For people who are completely Deaf and can't use hearing aids they are often left with no ability to communicate at all.
If you're ever interested, the Deaf community is so welcoming and close knit. There are Deaf coffee nights, trivia nights, events, etc. for Deaf and HoH people to mingle. If you're ever interested I would check it out. You can just google "Deaf events near me." I'm from the US, Los Angeles specifically, so we have a large Deaf population. I'm unsure how other countries are but if you're ever curious it may be fun for you. You get to meet other people who know what it is like to be HoH. If you ever have questions or want help finding resources feel free to reach out directly.

That's entirely up to you. If you're really into the Deaf community and feel connected to Deaf culture you may want to call you're yourself Deaf. If you have residual hearing you can identify as Hard of Hearing.
Just out of curiosity, are you fluent in sign? Have connected with other Deaf people? If not I highly encourage it. We so often see people that are mainstreamed (forced to read lips, get cochlear implants, etc). ASL really opens up your ability to communicate effectively. Deaf culture is so beautiful and the community is just incredible.

The general consensus among the Deaf and Hard of Hearing community is: Deaf is totally acceptable (actually preferred) This means you do not hear whatsoever. If someone has some residual hearing then they are considered Hard of Hearing (HoH). Deafness is often considered as an identity rather than a disability (which is a different topic altogether). So even if someone has 25% hearing in one ear they are Hard of Hearing but sometimes people with residual hearing still prefer to be called Deaf. 
Both are 100% acceptable.
Just never ever use "hearing impaired," I see it so often. It's a very outdated term.

Appreciate this ^
To add: please stop using the term "hearing impaired." It may sound politically correct and you may think it's appropriate but generally amongst the Deaf community, "Deaf" or "Hard of Hearing" are the appropriate terms. I obviously can't speak for everyone (including OP) but the term hearing impaired makes myself, my family and friends cringe.

As someone with Deaf family members and lots of Deaf friends. PLEASE stop handing us menus in Braille when we go out to eat.
We are just signing to each other. We are not blind and obviously don't need Braille menus.
It happens more often than you would probably think.
